rationale: A wins because it keeps the dangerous caveat in the headline: "Peloton posts its first profitable quarter in three years — on adjusted EBITDA, not net income" is the honest story, not the PR sugar version. B has usable bones, especially "Peloton Says It's Profitable. The Balance Sheet Tells a More Complicated Story.", but it keeps importing unsupplied narrative wallpaper like "The Target Customer Is Not Who Bought One in 2020" and "Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash." A is ready to guide a founder toward a real reporter; B needs a fact mop first.
gaps_in_A: "Peloton is selling bikes by the month now — the hardware company is becoming a subscription company" overstates the shift; Peloton already has membership economics in the supplied facts, so rental expansion is safer as an access or distribution story unless mix change is proven.
"$1,000+ hardware sale" is not in the company update. It may be true public context, but this blind set was supposed to trace every material claim to the given facts.

"The retention problem may be the one that's actually fixed" is a little too neat. Record-low churn needs the actual churn rate, denominator, and rental-program treatment before anyone calls the problem fixed.
gaps_in_B: "Peloton's CEO Cut $200M and Delivered the First Profit in Three Years" muddies adjusted EBITDA into "profit"; the update explicitly says Peloton remains net-unprofitable.
"The Target Customer Is Not Who Bought One in 2020" invents a customer-change claim. The update gives no buyer cohort, demographic shift, or rental uptake data.
"Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash" and "became symbols of pandemic excess and subsequent collapse" import an external cultural narrative not supplied in the update.
"More Loyal Subscribers Than Ever" and "What Keeps 6 Million Peloton Subscribers Paying" are two costumes for the same churn/member story, with one leaning on unsupported brand-collapse language.
